# Technical Brief: Database Storage and Transaction Internals

---

## 1. Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)

**Mechanism 1 — ARIES-style physiological logging with Log Sequence Numbers (LSNs).** ARIES (Mohan et al., 1992) logs *physiological* records: physical addressing to a page, logical description of the intra-page operation. Every log record carries a monotonically increasing **LSN**; every buffer-pool page stores a **pageLSN** recording the LSN of the last update applied to it. The WAL protocol is enforced by two invariants: (a) a dirty page may not be flushed until all log records up to its pageLSN are durable (**flushedLSN ≥ pageLSN**), and (b) **force-log-at-commit** — a transaction's commit record must be durable before acknowledging commit. This enables **STEAL/NO-FORCE** buffer management: dirty pages of uncommitted transactions may be evicted (steal), and committed pages need not be forced at commit (no-force), maximizing I/O flexibility. Each log record also carries a **prevLSN** back-pointer forming the per-transaction undo chain.

**Mechanism 2 — Group commit.** Forcing the log on every commit would bound throughput by the fsync latency of the device. Group commit batches the commit records of many concurrent transactions into a single log force: a committing transaction waits briefly while other commits accumulate, then one `fsync` durably persists all of them. InnoDB's `innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit`, PostgreSQL's `commit_delay`/`commit_siblings`, and the leader-follower group-commit design in MySQL 5.6+ binlog (binlog group commit with its flush/sync/commit stages) are concrete implementations. Group commit trades bounded commit latency for near-linear throughput scaling in fsync-bound workloads.

**Mechanism 3 — Fuzzy checkpointing.** A sharp checkpoint (quiescing all activity and flushing all dirty pages) causes latency spikes. ARIES instead takes **fuzzy checkpoints**: it writes `begin_checkpoint` and `end_checkpoint` records containing snapshots of the **Dirty Page Table (DPT)** (page → recLSN, the LSN that first dirtied the page) and the **Transaction Table (TT)** (txn → status, lastLSN), without flushing pages or pausing transactions. The **master record** points at the latest checkpoint, bounding the redo scan to min(recLSN) in the DPT. InnoDB performs analogous fuzzy checkpointing driven by the redo-log capacity (checkpoint age vs. `innodb_log_file_size`).

**Supporting mechanism — torn-page protection.** Because an 8–16 KB page write is not atomic on a 512 B/4 KB sector device, PostgreSQL writes **full-page images (full_page_writes)** on the first modification of a page after each checkpoint, and InnoDB uses the **doublewrite buffer**, writing pages first to a sequential staging area, so a torn page can be repaired from either the FPI or the doublewrite copy before redo is applied.

---

## 2. Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC)

**Mechanism 1 — PostgreSQL's in-place multi-versioning with xmin/xmax and VACUUM.** PostgreSQL stores versions as physical heap tuples. Each tuple header carries **xmin** (creating XID) and **xmax** (deleting/locking XID), plus hint bits and a **ctid** chain (with **HOT — Heap-Only Tuples** avoiding index churn when no indexed column changes). A statement or transaction takes a **snapshot** (xmin horizon, xmax, in-progress XID list); visibility is decided by comparing tuple xmin/xmax against the snapshot and the commit log (**pg_clog/pg_xact**). Dead versions are reclaimed asynchronously by **VACUUM**, which also performs **freezing** (setting FrozenTransactionId) to prevent **XID wraparound** — a hard correctness requirement given the 32-bit transaction ID space.

**Mechanism 2 — InnoDB's undo-log version chains with read views.** InnoDB updates records **in place** in the clustered index and stores prior versions as **undo log records** in **rollback segments**; each record carries hidden columns **DB_TRX_ID** and **DB_ROLL_PTR**, the latter pointing into the undo chain. A reader constructs a **read view** (low/high water marks plus active-transaction list at REPEATABLE READ snapshot time) and walks the roll-pointer chain backwards, materializing the newest version visible to it. Obsolete undo records are reclaimed by the background **purge** threads once no read view can need them (**history list length** measures purge lag). This contrasts with PostgreSQL: old versions live in a separate structure, so the main index stays compact, at the cost of undo-chain traversal for long-running readers.

**Mechanism 3 — Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI).** Plain Snapshot Isolation admits **write skew** anomalies (non-serializable histories with no write-write conflict). SSI (Cahill, Röhm, Fekete 2008; shipped in PostgreSQL 9.1) detects **rw-antidependencies** ("dangerous structures"): it tracks **SIREAD locks** (predicate-level, non-blocking) and aborts a transaction when it finds a pivot with both an incoming and an outgoing rw-antidependency edge among concurrent transactions — a necessary condition for any SI anomaly. This yields serializability with optimistic, abort-based enforcement rather than two-phase locking.

**Supporting mechanism — timestamp-ordered in-memory MVCC.** Microsoft **Hekaton** (SQL Server In-Memory OLTP) uses begin/end timestamps on versions, lock-free Bw-tree/hash indexes over version chains, and commit-time validation of read sets — showing MVCC adapted to latch-free main-memory designs.

---

## 3. LSM Trees (Log-Structured Merge Trees)

**Mechanism 1 — Memtable/SSTable flush pipeline.** Writes go to a durable WAL and an in-memory **memtable** (a skiplist in LevelDB/RocksDB, with concurrent-write variants). When full, the memtable becomes an **immutable memtable** and is flushed as a sorted, immutable **SSTable** (Sorted String Table) consisting of data blocks, an index block of **fence pointers** (first/last key per block), filter blocks, and a footer. The **MANIFEST/version-edit** log records which SSTables constitute each level, making the file-set itself recoverable.

**Mechanism 2 — Compaction policies: leveled vs. size-tiered.** **Leveled compaction** (RocksDB default, LevelDB) maintains levels L1…Ln of exponentially increasing capacity (typically 10×), each level (except L0) holding non-overlapping key ranges; compaction merges an L_i file with overlapping L_{i+1} files. It minimizes **space amplification** (~1.1×) and read amplification but maximizes **write amplification** (O(levels × fanout)). **Size-tiered compaction (STCS)** (Cassandra's default historically) merges similarly-sized runs, giving low write amplification but high space/read amplification due to overlapping runs. Cassandra's **TWCS** (time-window) and the **RUM conjecture / Monkey** (Dayan et al.) formalize the read/update/memory trade-off and optimal per-level filter-bit allocation.

**Mechanism 3 — Bloom filters and tombstone-based deletion.** Point lookups must consult every sorted run that might contain the key; a per-SSTable (or per-block, prefix) **Bloom filter** answers "definitely absent" with a tunable false-positive rate (~1% at 10 bits/key), collapsing most negative lookups to zero I/O. Deletes cannot mutate immutable SSTables, so they write **tombstones** — markers that shadow older versions during the **merging iterator**'s k-way merge across memtable and runs. Tombstones may only be dropped during a compaction that reaches the bottommost level containing the key (Cassandra additionally gates on **gc_grace_seconds** to avoid resurrecting deletes in a replicated setting). Range deletes use dedicated **range tombstones** (RocksDB `DeleteRange`).

---

## 4. B+Tree Maintenance

**Mechanism 1 — Split, merge, and redistribution with underflow handling.** Insertion into a full leaf triggers a **node split**: half the keys move to a new right sibling, and a **separator key** is posted to the parent, possibly splitting recursively up to the root (the only way tree height grows). Deletion causing underflow (below ~50% fill) is repaired by **redistribution (key rotation)** from a sibling through the parent separator, or by **merging (coalescing)** siblings and deleting the parent separator. Many production engines (e.g., classic InnoDB/PostgreSQL behavior) deliberately use **lazy deletion** — tolerating underfull pages and reclaiming only fully empty ones — since workloads often reinsert. Related structural optimizations: **suffix truncation** of separator keys (store the shortest string separating the subtrees) and **prefix compression** within pages.

**Mechanism 2 — Latch coupling (crabbing) and optimistic descent.** Concurrent traversal uses **latch coupling**: acquire the child's latch before releasing the parent's. Pessimistic writers hold write latches down the path, releasing ancestors only when a child is **"safe"** (not full for insert, not half-empty for delete), so splits/merges cannot propagate above the latched frontier. The **optimistic protocol** descends with read latches assuming no structure modification, write-latching only the leaf, and restarts in pessimistic mode on the rare unsafe case. Modern variants use **optimistic lock coupling** (version-validated, latch-free reads, as in LeanStore/Umbra).

**Mechanism 3 — Lehman–Yao B-link trees.** The **B^link-tree** (Lehman & Yao 1981) adds to every node a **right-sibling pointer** and a **high key** (upper bound of the node's key range). A split is decomposed into two atomic steps: create the right sibling and link it, then post the separator to the parent. A concurrent reader that lands on a node whose high key is below its search key simply **"moves right"** along the sibling chain — so readers never need to latch more than one node at a time and tolerate in-progress splits. PostgreSQL's nbtree is a Lehman–Yao implementation (with deletion handled per Lanin–Shasha-style techniques and page recycling deferred until no scan can hold a pointer to the page). Related modern descendant: the latch-free **Bw-tree** (delta records + mapping table + CAS), used in Hekaton range indexes.

**Supporting mechanism — bulk loading.** Building a B+tree from sorted input bottom-up packs leaves at a chosen fill factor and constructs internal levels in one pass, avoiding the random splits of repeated insertion.

---

## 5. Two-Phase Commit (2PC)

**Mechanism 1 — The base protocol with forced log writes.** The **coordinator** sends `PREPARE`; each **participant** that can commit force-writes a **prepare record** (entering the **prepared/in-doubt state**, retaining all locks) and votes YES; a participant voting NO may unilaterally abort. On unanimous YES the coordinator force-writes its **commit record — the commit point** — then sends `COMMIT`; participants force a commit record and ACK; the coordinator writes a non-forced **end record**, allowing it to forget the transaction. The forced writes are exactly what makes each role's promise recoverable: a prepared participant must be able to go either way after a crash and must ask the coordinator (**termination protocol**) for the outcome. The X/Open **XA** interface standardizes these roles (TM/RM, `xa_prepare`, `xa_commit`, `xa_recover`).

**Mechanism 2 — Presumed Abort and Presumed Commit.** In **presumed abort (PA)** — the variant standardized in practice (R*, Mohan/Lindsay/Obermarck 1986) — the coordinator writes *no* log record for aborts and forgets aborted transactions immediately; a participant inquiring about an unknown transaction is answered "abort" by presumption. This removes forced abort records and all abort ACKs. **Presumed commit (PC)** inverts the presumption to optimize the common commit case, eliminating participant commit-ACKs, but requires the coordinator to force a **collecting/initiation record before the prepare phase** so that a coordinator crash cannot cause a false commit presumption — a subtle but essential correctness detail (addressed more cheaply by "new presumed commit," Lampson & Lomet).

**Mechanism 3 — Read-only optimization and the blocking problem with Paxos Commit / 3PC.** A participant that performed no writes replies **READ-ONLY** to prepare, releases its locks immediately, writes nothing, and is excluded from phase two. The fundamental weakness of 2PC is **blocking**: if the coordinator fails after participants prepare, in-doubt participants hold locks indefinitely (cooperative termination — querying peer participants — helps only if some peer knows the outcome). **Three-phase commit (3PC, Skeen)** inserts a `PRE-COMMIT` round to make the protocol non-blocking under crash-stop failures with a synchronous network, but it is unsafe under network partitions and is rarely deployed. The production-grade remedy is **Paxos Commit** (Gray & Lamport): replicate the commit decision (or each participant's vote) via a consensus group, making the "coordinator" a replicated state machine — the pattern used by **Google Spanner** (2PC layered over per-shard Paxos groups) and most modern distributed SQL systems (CockroachDB's parallel commit being a further pipelined refinement).

---

## 6. Logical Clocks

**Mechanism 1 — Lamport clocks.** Lamport (1978) defines the **happened-before** partial order (→) and a scalar counter: increment on each local event; on message receipt set `C := max(C, C_msg) + 1`. This guarantees **a → b ⇒ C(a) < C(b)** (consistency with causality) but not the converse: Lamport timestamps cannot distinguish causal order from concurrency. Breaking ties with process IDs yields a **total order**, the basis of Lamport's mutual-exclusion algorithm and of totally-ordered multicast; databases use the same idea in commit-timestamp generation and last-writer-wins registers.

**Mechanism 2 — Vector clocks and dotted version vectors.** A **vector clock** (Fidge/Mattern, 1988) keeps one counter per process; comparison is pointwise, and it **characterizes causality exactly**: VC(a) < VC(b) ⟺ a → b, with incomparable vectors identifying **concurrent** events. **Version vectors** apply this to replica state to detect conflicting siblings (Dynamo-style stores). **Dotted version vectors (DVVs)** (Preguiça et al.) extend version vectors with a discrete "dot" for the latest event, fixing the **sibling explosion / false-concurrency** problem when clients write through different coordinators — adopted by **Riak**. The cost is O(replicas) metadata and pruning complexity.

**Mechanism 3 — Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC).** HLC (Kulkarni et al., 2014) combines a physical component `l` (max physical time observed) with a bounded logical component `c` for tie-breaking, satisfying both the Lamport property and **closeness to physical time** (|l − pt| bounded by clock skew ε). HLC timestamps fit in 64 bits, are monotone across message exchange, and enable consistent snapshots without waiting. **CockroachDB** and **YugabyteDB** use HLC for MVCC timestamps and (in Cockroach's case) an **uncertainty interval** [ts, ts + max_offset] within which reads may need to restart.

**Mechanism 4 — TrueTime and commit wait.** Google **Spanner**'s **TrueTime** API returns an interval `TT.now() = [earliest, latest]` bounding true time via GPS/atomic-clock time masters. A transaction commits at timestamp `s = TT.now().latest` and then performs **commit wait**: it delays acknowledging until `TT.after(s)`, guaranteeing s has passed everywhere. This yields **external consistency (strict serializability)** with globally meaningful timestamps — effectively trading ~2ε of commit latency for the elimination of logical-clock metadata propagation.

---

## 7. Quorum Systems

**Mechanism 1 — Weighted voting with intersecting read/write quorums (Gifford, 1979).** Each replica holds votes; a read quorum R and write quorum W must satisfy **R + W > N** (read/write intersection ⇒ every read sees the latest write, identified via version numbers) and **W > N/2** (write/write intersection ⇒ no two conflicting writes both succeed). Tuning (R=1, W=N) vs. (R=N, W=1) trades read vs. write availability; weights allow heterogeneous replicas and **witnesses** (vote-only, data-less replicas). This is the ancestral model behind Cassandra/Riak **tunable consistency** levels (ONE, QUORUM, LOCAL_QUORUM, ALL) — with the caveat that without consensus, R+W>N alone gives regular/atomic-register semantics only with careful read-repair/write-back (ABD-style), not full linearizable multi-object transactions.

**Mechanism 2 — Sloppy quorums, hinted handoff, and anti-entropy (Dynamo).** Amazon **Dynamo** prioritizes availability: if home replicas in the **preference list** are unreachable, writes are accepted by the next healthy nodes on the consistent-hashing ring (**sloppy quorum**) which store a **hinted handoff** — the write plus the identity of the intended owner — and deliver it when the owner recovers. Because sloppy quorums break strict intersection, durability/consistency is restored in the background by **anti-entropy**: replicas exchange **Merkle trees** per key range to find divergent keys cheaply, and **read repair** writes the reconciled (version-vector-merged) value back to stale replicas on the read path. Cassandra implements all three mechanisms essentially as described.

**Mechanism 3 — Flexible quorums in consensus (Flexible Paxos).** Howard, Malkhi & Spiegelman (2016) showed that Paxos does not require majority quorums in both phases — only that **every phase-1 (leader election) quorum intersects every phase-2 (replication) quorum** (|Q1| + |Q2| > N); phase-2 quorums need not intersect each other. This permits, e.g., N=5 with |Q2|=2 for fast steady-state replication at the cost of |Q1|=4 on leader change, and underlies **grid quorums** and leader-leases designs; Raft's joint-consensus membership change and systems like Kafka's KRaft reason with the same intersection framework. Related construction: **quorum leases / Megastore-style per-replica read quorums** for local reads.

---

## 8. Crash Recovery

**Mechanism 1 — ARIES three-phase recovery.** On restart from the last checkpoint: (i) **Analysis** scans forward, reconstructing the Dirty Page Table and Transaction Table, identifying **loser transactions** and the **redoLSN** = min(recLSN). (ii) **Redo** implements **repeating history**: *every* logged update — including those of losers — is reapplied if `pageLSN < LSN`, restoring the exact pre-crash state; the pageLSN test makes redo **idempotent**. (iii) **Undo** rolls back losers in reverse LSN order, writing a **Compensation Log Record (CLR)** for each undone action; the CLR's **undoNextLSN** pointer skips already-undone work, guaranteeing **bounded, non-redone undo** even across repeated crashes during recovery (CLRs are redo-only, never undone). This triad — repeating history, CLRs, physiological idempotent redo — is what makes STEAL/NO-FORCE safe, and it is the template for InnoDB, SQL Server, and DB2 recovery.

**Mechanism 2 — Shadow paging.** System R's original recovery (Lorie 1977) and modern **copy-on-write** engines (LMDB, older SQLite-adjacent designs, ZFS at the FS level) never overwrite live pages: updates go to **shadow (new) pages**, and commit is a single atomic installation of a new **page-table/root pointer** (flip of the master root). Recovery is trivial — the old root is intact, uncommitted shadows are garbage — giving instant restart with no redo/undo. Costs: page-grained copy amplification, loss of physical clustering, garbage collection of superseded pages, and awkward concurrency (System R needed logging anyway for record-level locking), which is why pure shadow paging lost to WAL in update-heavy engines, surviving in single-writer MVCC stores like **LMDB** (two root pointers, alternating).

**Mechanism 3 — Journal-based recovery: SQLite rollback journal vs. WAL mode.** SQLite's **rollback journal** is **undo-only, FORCE/STEAL-ish**: before modifying a page, the original page image is written to the journal and synced; commit flushes the database and invalidates the journal (**commit point = journal header invalidation/deletion**); recovery replays the journal to roll the database *back*. SQLite's **WAL mode** inverts this into **redo-only logging**: new page versions are appended to the WAL, the main database is untouched until **checkpoint** copies frames back; the commit point is a commit frame in the WAL, readers use the **wal-index (shm)** to find the latest committed frame per page, giving readers-don't-block-writers semantics. Recovery = scan WAL for valid frames up to the last commit frame (validated by per-frame **checksums/salts**) — a clean illustration of undo vs. redo journaling trade-offs.

**Supporting mechanism — torn-write repair and LSM recovery.** InnoDB's **doublewrite buffer** repairs torn pages before redo (redo is physiological and needs intact pages); PostgreSQL's **full-page writes** make redo self-contained after checkpoints. LSM engines recover by replaying the memtable WAL and reconstructing the live file set from the **MANIFEST** log — recovery of *metadata* by logging, recovery of *data* by immutability.

---

## Synthesis

A unifying lens: every durable system must make one **atomic commit point** (a forced commit record, a root-pointer flip, a quorum of acks, a Paxos decision) and arrange that everything before it is **redoable or discardable** and everything after it is **replayable and idempotent** (pageLSN tests, CLRs, immutable SSTables, version intersection). MVCC and logical clocks generalize the same idea in the time dimension — ordering and visibility derived from monotone counters — while quorums and 2PC/Paxos-commit generalize it in the space dimension, replacing a single forced disk write with an intersecting set of acknowledgments.

Answer: The complete technical brief is given above, covering all eight areas — WAL (ARIES physiological logging/LSNs, group commit, fuzzy checkpoints, full-page writes/doublewrite), MVCC (PostgreSQL xmin/xmax+VACUUM, InnoDB undo chains+read views+purge, SSI, Hekaton), LSM trees (memtable/SSTable flush, leveled vs. size-tiered compaction, Bloom filters+tombstones/merge iterators), B+tree maintenance (split/merge/redistribution, latch crabbing/optimistic descent, Lehman–Yao B-link trees, bulk loading), 2PC (forced-log base protocol/XA, presumed abort/commit, read-only optimization, 3PC/Paxos Commit), logical clocks (Lamport, vector/dotted version vectors, HLC, TrueTime commit-wait), quorums (Gifford weighted voting R+W>N, Dynamo sloppy quorums/hinted handoff/Merkle anti-entropy, Flexible Paxos), and crash recovery (ARIES analysis/redo/undo with CLRs, shadow paging, SQLite rollback-journal vs. WAL-mode recovery) — each with three or more named mechanisms treated in depth.
